subsystem: Guardrails B — human-in-the-loop approval (packages/server/src/guardrails/) + untrusted-content labelling & managed-secret egress (packages/core/src/secrets/, packages/server/src/guardrails/)
summary: Two halves, one idea each. For approval: the pending row IS the ticket. A held SSE call and a "retry after approval" both resolve to the same atomic `UPDATE approval_request ... WHERE status='approved'` — so option (a) HOLD, option (b) machine-readable deny, and option (c) pre-approval are one table and one predicate, not three mechanisms, and the whole thing is forward-compatible with MRTR without a schema change. The approval row never stores raw arguments, only a redacted projection; full arguments exist only in memory while a call is actually held, so the queue can never become the secret archive the audit design already refuses to be. For untrusted content: we ship exactly two real controls — a nonce-delimited provenance label that only helps clients choosing to honour it, and a literal-value match of credentials we ourselves manage — and we name generic prompt-injection detection and generic PII/secret regex as theatre and refuse them. Everything else about a result (bytes, blocks, link counts, odd URL schemes, declared mime types) is reported to the operator, never blocked on. Guardrails live entirely in packages/server and evaluate strictly after `resolveTool`, so a guardrail error can never distinguish a hidden tool from a missing one.
phase: Split. B2 (provenance labelling, `findManagedSecrets`, result-shape reporting, the two counters, the `result_shape`/`secret_hits` audit fields) lands in **P4 observability, +0.5 dev-weeks** because it rides the audit and metrics wiring already being built there and needs no new UI. B1 (approval protocol, `approval_request`, the `approval` SSE frame, the queue screen, the CLI) lands in **P7 hardening, +1.0 dev-weeks** because it needs the P1 call path, the P2 scope invariant and the P3 console shell to already exist. Total **+1.5 dev-weeks → 14.0**.

decisions.decision: v1 ships (a) HOLD, with the approval row doubling as a single-use ticket so (b) and (c) fall out for free. Constants: hold 300_000 ms (`MCPR_APPROVAL_HOLD_MS`), keep-alive 15_000 ms reusing the existing `MCPR_SSE_KEEPALIVE_MS`, pending row TTL 900_000 ms, ticket TTL after approval 600_000 ms. On timeout or client disconnect the row stays `pending`; a later approval becomes a ticket that the caller's next identical call consumes instantly.
decisions.rationale: Three protocols collapse to one table and one atomic UPDATE, because 'the operator said yes' and 'the caller is still waiting' are independent facts. The SDK's default client request timeout is 60 s, so a meaningful share of holds will be abandoned by the client regardless — the ticket is what makes that survivable instead of a dead end.
decisions.cost: A held call holds an HTTP connection and an SSE stream for up to 5 minutes. The upgrade is MRTR (SEP-2322): when the SDK ships 2026-07-28 the hold becomes an `InputRequiredResult` with `inputRequests` and the client's `inputResponses` retry consumes the same ticket — zero schema change.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub has no approval path at all. The naive implementation is a boolean `requiresApproval` on the tool plus a blocking in-memory promise map; that loses every pending decision on restart, gives the caller nothing machine-readable on timeout, and has no way to express 'approved, but the caller already left'.

decisions.decision: `approval_request` has NO raw-arguments column. It stores `args_preview` (a redacted leaf projection, DB-capped at 8 KB) and `args_bytes`. Full arguments exist only in the holding process's memory, so `GET /api/approvals/:id/args` works only while `held = true`, requires `audit:payload:read` on top of the operator role, and writes an `approval.args.read` audit event.
decisions.rationale: The settled audit design defaults to `metadata` precisely because verbatim payload storage makes a table the highest-value target; an approval queue full of pending write-calls would be strictly worse, since those arguments are the ones most likely to carry live credentials. Binding reveal to the in-flight hold makes the retention window structurally zero rather than policy-zero.
decisions.cost: An operator deciding on an abandoned card sees only the redacted projection. Acceptable: the projection keeps scalar values under 256 chars verbatim, which is what actually drives the decision (which repo, which path, which recipient).

decisions.decision: Guardrails run strictly AFTER `engine.resolveTool` succeeds and after `checkGrant`. Core gains exactly two public methods — `resolveTool(scope, principal, name)` and `callResolved(tool, args, {signal})` — and `callTool` becomes their composition. No policy, approval, operator or HTTP concept enters packages/core.
decisions.rationale: The one-place `ToolUnavailableError` invariant must hold: a caller who is policy-denied has already passed `isExposed`, so the different error shape leaks nothing they could not learn from `tools/list`. Splitting resolve from call is the minimum seam that gives the server the server/tool/schema it needs for the fingerprint and the audit row.
decisions.cost: Two methods on core's public API instead of one. No new interface, no hook, no injected policy object — the server calls them in order.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub interleaves filtering, group re-injection and dispatch inside a 5006-line `mcpService.ts`, which is exactly why their disable check had to be re-added at execution time as a CVE fix (afcc72f) and why it has to look under both bare and prefixed keys (mcpService.ts:3388).

decisions.decision: An approval-pending call does NOT count against the per-principal concurrency semaphore of 8. It releases its slot on entering the hold and takes a token from a separate pending budget: 3 per principal, 50 globally. On approval it re-acquires an execution slot with a 10 s budget, re-runs `checkGrant` + `resolveTool`, then consumes the ticket, then dispatches.
decisions.rationale: A held call is doing no work — no upstream socket, no CPU — so charging it an execution slot would let three slow approvals starve a principal's real traffic. The separate, much smaller budget is simultaneously the concurrency fix and the operator-flood rate limit, which is why it is one counter and not two features.
decisions.cost: Two counters instead of one. Re-acquire order is load-bearing: slot → re-check → consume → dispatch, so a failed re-acquire (429) never burns a single-use ticket.

decisions.decision: Approvers are `operator` or `admin`, checked as the existing route-group middleware. All four approval routes reject any principal whose kind is not `user` — an API key, including a compromised one, can never approve anything. Self-approval is ALLOWED by default, always stamped `self_approved: true` on the row, the audit event and the card; `guardrails.requireSecondPerson` (default false) turns it into a 403.
decisions.rationale: A named approver set would be a second authorization axis, which the project owner already collapsed to one; role plus the API-key exclusion gives the same protection with columns we already have. Forbidding self-approval by default would make the feature unusable for a two-person self-hosted team, which is the deployment we target.
decisions.cost: With `requireSecondPerson = true` and exactly one admin, every approval deadlocks until a second human exists. Stated in the setting's own `.describe()`, which the generated Settings screen renders.

decisions.decision: There is no 'approve all' control anywhere in the UI or the API. The only bulk affordance is `scope: 'tool'` — approve this exact (principal, server, tool) triple for 15 or 60 minutes, TTL from a fixed enum, never free-form — which auto-resolves every queued card matching that triple. Additionally, a denied `call_hash` enters a 10-minute cooldown during which identical retries are refused without creating a card, and an identical pending `call_hash` joins the existing card (`waiters++`) instead of making a second one.
decisions.rationale: Fatigue attacks work by volume, so the answer is to make repeats free to dismiss rather than to make dismissal cheap: dedup kills the identical-call flood, the per-principal cap of 3 kills the varied-args flood, and the cooldown means a deny costs the attacker ten minutes. A bounded window grant is the affordance an operator actually wants at 3am and it still cannot escape one tool and one caller.
decisions.cost: A caller can perturb arguments to get a fresh `call_hash` and dodge the cooldown — but only back into a capped queue, where the new card is visibly near-identical to the denied one.

decisions.decision: Provenance labelling is `_meta['io.mcprouter/provenance']` ALWAYS, and content-block wrapping only when `guardrails.labelling = 'meta+wrap'` (default `'meta'`). Wrapping adds exactly two text blocks around the untouched upstream array, delimited by a per-result 110-bit nonce so upstream text cannot forge the closing marker. The `[mcprouter:truncated N bytes]` marker is gateway-authored and is therefore emitted OUTSIDE the envelope, after the closing block.
decisions.rationale: `_meta` is the spec's place for out-of-band annotation and mutates nothing, so it is always safe; injecting text blocks breaks clients that expect exactly one block or JSON.parse the first one, so it is opt-in. The nonce is the only part that is not decorative — without it, upstream content can emit a closing marker and escape the envelope.
decisions.cost: This helps only clients that choose to honour it, and no client honours it today. We say that in the setting's description rather than pretending otherwise.
decisions.mcphub_contrast: mcphub marks only its own compressed results (`[mcphub:compressed-tool-result …]`, toolResultCompressionService.ts:444) and never distinguishes gateway text from upstream text. The naive version is a fixed ASCII delimiter, which upstream content can trivially emit itself.

decisions.decision: Egress scanning matches ONLY literal values of credentials we manage (plus their base64 and percent-encoded forms), for values ≥ 16 characters, and BLOCKS by default (`guardrails.secretEgress: block | require_approval | report`). We refuse generic PII regexes, generic secret-shape regexes, and any prompt-injection heuristic over tool results — those are the same false confidence we already rejected for audit redaction.
decisions.rationale: A literal multi-string match of values we own has no false-confidence problem: a hit means the argument genuinely contains that exact credential, which is the exfiltration we exist to stop, and the error names the secret label and the JSON pointer so the fix is one step. A pattern matcher has no such property, and a gateway cannot in any case control how the client's model frames text it receives.
decisions.cost: Misses secrets split across two arguments, chained encodings, and values under 16 chars. The false-positive escape hatch is one boolean, `secrets.scan_egress`, settable from the server edit screen and named in the block message.

decisions.decision: `findManagedSecrets` lives in `packages/core/src/secrets/resolver.ts` — the module that already caches resolved plaintext for connect — and exports only the predicate. Plaintext values never leave that module; the matcher is one compiled RegExp alternation of escaped literals, rebuilt when the resolved-config cache is invalidated.
decisions.rationale: The settled rule is that nothing but the resolver may read `secrets`, so a second reader for the guardrail would be the actual violation; putting the matcher where the values already legitimately live is both the smaller diff and the smaller blast radius. If the resolver cannot load secrets, the server has no upstreams, so there is no new failure mode to design.
decisions.cost: A string matcher in `packages/core`. Legitimate: core forbids HTTP, sessions and authz decisions, not pure functions — and `SecretHit` carries ids, labels and paths, never a value.

decisions.decision: Every guardrail refusal is a `CallToolResult` with `isError: true`, a flat text block and `_meta['io.mcprouter/guardrail']`, at HTTP 200 — not a JSON-RPC error. Reasons: `policy_deny | approval_pending | approval_denied | approval_timeout | approval_queue_full | approval_cooldown | secret_egress | guardrail_unavailable`.
decisions.rationale: A JSON-RPC error makes the SDK throw and many hosts abort the whole turn, which is the 'model does something worse' failure the brief warns about; an `isError` result is delivered to the model as tool output, which is the only way the retry-after-approval path can ever be taken. `ToolUnavailableError` stays a JSON-RPC error, and that difference leaks nothing because guardrails only run on tools the caller can already list.
decisions.cost: Two error idioms on one endpoint. The text is deliberately instruction-free and never suggests an alternative tool, so it cannot steer a model into a workaround.

interfaces.name: guardedCall — the chosen approval protocol, as a sequence
interfaces.sketch:
POST /mcp | /mcp/g/:group | /mcp/s/:server | /mcp/smart[/g/:group]   (tools/call)

 1  authenticate            -> principal: Principal  (session | apiKey | oauth)
 2  gateway.resolveTarget   -> scope: ResolvedScope
 3  checkGrant(principal, scope)                       -- 403, unchanged
 4  sem.acquire(principalKey)                          -- default 8, else 429 Retry-After: 1
 5  resolved = engine.resolveTool(scope, principal, exposedName)
       throws ToolUnavailableError -> `Tool not found: ${name}`   (byte-identical, ALWAYS first)
 5a $smart dispatch: the `call_tool` meta-tool re-enters HERE with the INNER tool name.
       It calls guardedCall(), NOT engine.callTool(). <- the bypass that is easy to miss
 6  hits = findManagedSecrets(args)                    -- B2 egress, core predicate
       hits && mode='block'            -> deny('secret_egress')  + audit guardrail.blocked
       hits && mode='require_approval' -> goto 8 with reason='secret_egress'
       hits && mode='report'           -> record on the audit row, continue
 7  decision = policy.evaluate({principal, scope, resolved, args})   -- OTHER AGENT
       'allow' -> 10 | 'deny' -> deny('policy_deny') | 'require_approval' -> 8
       throws / unreachable -> deny('guardrail_unavailable')          FAIL CLOSED
 8  callHash = sha256(canonicalJson({s: serverId, t: bareName, a: args})).slice(0,32)
 8a ticket = consumeTicket(principalId, serverId, bareName, callHash)  -- atomic, below
       hit -> audit approval.consumed; goto 10
 8b recentDeny(principalId, callHash) within denyCooldownMs -> deny('approval_cooldown')
 8c pendingFor(principalId) >= 3  ||  pendingGlobal >= 50 -> deny('approval_queue_full')
 8d row = INSERT approval_request ... ON CONFLICT (principal_id, call_hash) WHERE status='pending'
            DO UPDATE SET waiters = approval_request.waiters + 1
          RETURNING *;                       -- identical pending call JOINS the card
       if inserted: emit SSE {t:'approval', op:'new'}; fire webhook (2 s, fire-and-forget)
                    audit approval.requested
 9  HOLD  (only if this request created or joined a card)
       switch the response to text/event-stream:
         Content-Type: text/event-stream; Cache-Control: no-cache; X-Accel-Buffering: no
       sem.release(principalKey)                    <- the held call frees its slot NOW
       pendingBudget.acquire(principalKey)          <- separate counter, cap 3
       every 15_000 ms:  write ":\r\n"              <- SSE comment, protocol-invisible
         AND, only if the request carried _meta.progressToken:
           notifications/progress { progressToken, progress: elapsedSec, total: 300,
                                    message: 'awaiting operator approval' }
       await Promise.race([ decided, AbortSignal.timeout(300_000), c.req.raw.signal ])
         approved -> sem.acquire (10 s budget, else 429)
                  -> re-run checkGrant + resolveTool   <- key revoked / tool disabled mid-wait
                  -> consumeTicket (atomic)  -> 10
         denied   -> deny('approval_denied', note)  on the stream, close
         timeout  -> deny('approval_timeout', approvalId); row stays pending until expires_at
         abort    -> UPDATE ... SET held=false; stop holding; NO deny, NO decision
10  result = engine.callResolved(resolved, args, { signal })
11  shape = inspectResult(result)                     -- B2 reporting
    result = truncate(result, 1 MB - 512 B reserve)   -- settled
    result = label(result, provenance, shape)         -- B2 labelling
    audit tool.call { approvalId?, secretHits?, resultShape: shape }

Gateway restart mid-hold: in-memory waiters die, clients see a dropped stream (= cancellation
by definition), rows stay `pending` with held=false. Boot does nothing special; the 30 s sweep
expires them at expires_at. An operator can still decide, and the decision becomes a ticket.
interfaces.notes: Step 5 before steps 6-8 is the invariant that keeps a guardrail error from distinguishing a hidden tool from a missing one. Step 5a is the single highest-value bypass fix in this design.

interfaces.name: approval_request (Drizzle)
interfaces.notes: Deliberately no `args` / `args_sealed` column. The retry path does not need stored arguments — the caller resends them and `call_hash` matches — and the hold path already has them in memory. That makes the retention window for raw arguments structurally zero.

interfaces.name: secrets.scan_egress (column addition)
interfaces.notes: One column, not an exception table. A per-(server, tool, secret) exception model is rule-engine territory and belongs to the other agent if it is ever needed.

interfaces.name: GuardrailResult — the deny payload
interfaces.notes: Every string is flat and instruction-free: no suggestion of an alternative tool, no hint at what would pass. `ToolUnavailableError` remains a JSON-RPC error and is unaffected.

interfaces.name: ApprovalFrame — the new SSE frame on GET /api/events
interfaces.notes: NOBODY WATCHING: nothing rescues the call — it times out at 300 s and denies closed. Two cheap mitigations, both real: one fire-and-forget webhook (`guardrails.webhookUrl`, 2 s timeout, SSRF-validated by the same `assertSafeUrl` as upstream URLs, failures logged not fatal, body carries id/server/tool/principal/reason and no arguments), and `mcprouter approvals` in the CLI so an on-call operator needs no browser.

interfaces.name: Approval routes
interfaces.sketch:
GET    /api/approvals?status=pending&server=&principal=&limit=50   operator|admin
         -> ApprovalCard[] including argsPreview
GET    /api/approvals/:id                                          operator|admin
POST   /api/approvals/:id/decide                                   operator|admin
         body: { decision: 'approve'|'deny',
                 scope?: 'call'|'tool',        // default 'call'
                 ttl?: '15m'|'60m',            // only with scope:'tool', fixed enum
                 note?: string }               // <= 280 chars
         409 + the winning decision if the row is no longer `pending`
GET    /api/approvals/:id/args                                     operator|admin
         + permission `audit:payload:read`; 410 Gone unless held=true
         -> { args: unknown }  and an approval.args.read audit event

ALL FOUR reject principal.kind !== 'user' with 403 before any other check.
A compromised mcpr_ key cannot approve, cannot list the queue, cannot reveal arguments.

// decide handler, the part that matters:
const [row] = await db.update(approvalRequest)
  .set({ status: d === 'approve' ? 'approved' : 'denied', decidedAt: sql`now()`,
         decidedBy: me.id, decidedByName: me.name, decisionNote: note,
         grantScope: scope ?? 'call',
         selfApproved: await ownsPrincipal(me.id, row.principalKind, row.principalId),
         expiresAt: d === 'approve'
           ? sql`now() + ${ttlMs(scope, ttl)}::interval` : sql`now()` })
  .where(and(eq(approvalRequest.id, id), eq(approvalRequest.status, 'pending')))
  .returning();
if (!row) return c.json(await current(id), 409);       // two operators, one winner
if (cfg.requireSecondPerson && row.selfApproved) -> 403, row stays pending
notifyWaiters(row); emit({t:'approval', op:'decided', ...}); audit('approval.decided', row);
if (scope === 'tool') resolveQueuedDuplicates(row);    // the ONLY bulk affordance
interfaces.notes: `scope:'tool'` resolution is a follow-up UPDATE over pending rows matching (principal_id, server_id, tool_name); each resolved row gets its own `approval.decided` audit event with `viaGrant: <id>` so a window grant never hides what it approved.

interfaces.name: Approval card + queue screen
interfaces.sketch:
Route /approvals · sidebar item `APPROVALS` with a count badge fed by ['approvals','count'].
Deep link to one card via the existing inspector param: ?inspect=approval:<id>. No modal stack.

  PENDING 7   OLDEST 02:41   [server ▾] [caller ▾] [rule ▾]        (no bulk control exists)

  ┌ APPROVAL ─────────────────────────────────────────── 04:12 left ─┐
  │ ● PENDING   github__create_issue                                 │
  │   server  github              group  eng-tools                   │
  │   caller  ci-bot   apikey mcpr_…7f3a   ·   10.2.0.14             │
  │   rule    write-tools-need-approval    ·   2 calls waiting       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ARGUMENTS   redacted projection · raw values are never stored    │
  │   /owner       "clearer-io"                                      │
  │   /repo        "billing"                                         │
  │   /title       "Rotate prod keys"                                │
  │   /body        "Following the incident on…"   str(8134)   ✂      │
  │   /token       «secret: github.PAT»                       ⚠      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ [ Reveal arguments ]   audit:payload:read · logged · held only   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ note ▸ [_______________________________________________] 0/280   │
  │ [ Deny ]              [ Approve once ]   [ Approve 15m ▾ ]       │
  │                        ⚠ your own key — this is a self-approval  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Aesthetic: dense grid, mono for every identifier through the <Id> component (enforced by the
local ESLint rule), status dot amber pending / green approved / red denied / grey expired,
all four measured against WCAG AA. Countdown from expiresAt, computed client-side.

Accessibility (not negotiable):
  · <article role="group" aria-labelledby={`ap-${id}-h`}>; the countdown is aria-live="off"
    and a polite summary is announced only when status changes, so 7 cards do not shout.
  · Approve / Deny are real <button>; the 15m/60m picker is a shadcn DropdownMenu.
  · "Approve 15m" opens an alert-dialog (the one layer we allow) stating the exact grant:
    "ci-bot may call github__create_issue with any arguments until 14:27."
  · Reveal is an inline expansion of the same card — never a modal. One inspector param, no stacking.
  · A card whose caller has disconnected shows `caller gone · decision becomes a 10m ticket`.
interfaces.notes: What the approver must NOT be shown by default: raw argument values over 256 chars, and any value matching a managed secret — both replaced in the projection before it is ever written to Postgres, not masked in the renderer.

interfaces.name: label() — provenance marker and its interaction with truncation
interfaces.notes: Default is `'meta'`. `'meta+wrap'` is opt-in because two extra text blocks break clients that expect exactly one block or parse the first one as JSON. A per-server override is deferred.

interfaces.name: findManagedSecrets — the egress matcher
interfaces.notes: The one runnable check, packages/core/src/secrets/resolver.test.ts: literal / base64 / urlencoded each hit; a 15-char value does not; `scanEgress:false` does not; the returned SecretHit has no `value` key (asserted with Object.keys). Node's test runner, no fixtures.

interfaces.name: inspectResult — the cheap, real, REPORT-ONLY controls
interfaces.notes: Nothing here blocks. Every one of these is a signal an operator can act on, and none of them has a defensible blocking threshold.

interfaces.name: Audit events
interfaces.sketch:
Five new `evt` values, all reusing audit_event's existing columns — no new table.
Every one carries: requestId, traceId, principalKind/Id/Name, sourceIp, serverId/Slug,
toolName, exposedName, groupSlug, outcome, durationMs.

evt='approval.requested'   outcome='blocked'
  + approvalId, reason, ruleId, callHash, argsBytes, inputKeys (top-level key names),
    secretHits[] (ids/labels/paths, never values)
  Written ONCE per card. A joined waiter bumps `waiters` and writes nothing.

evt='approval.decided'     outcome='ok' | 'denied'
  + approvalId, decidedBy, decidedByName, selfApproved, grantScope, ttlMs,
    decisionNote, waiters, held, viaGrant? (set on rows resolved by a tool-scope window)

evt='approval.expired'     outcome='expired'
  + approvalId, waiters, held, consumed=false, ageMs

evt='approval.args.read'   outcome='ok'
  + approvalId, readerId, readerName, leafCount
  The ONLY event that records a look at raw arguments. Reuses `audit:payload:read`.

evt='guardrail.blocked'    outcome='blocked'
  + errorReason ∈ { secret_egress, approval_queue_full, approval_cooldown,
                    guardrail_unavailable }, callHash, secretHits[]

And the existing evt='tool.call' gains two fields in its jsonb:
  approvalId?   — the ticket that unblocked it (hold or retry, indistinguishable here)
  resultShape   — ResultShape from inspectResult

All of it goes through the settled bounded queue (cap 10 000, flushed every 250 ms or at
200 rows) EXCEPT approval.decided and approval.args.read, which are written synchronously
inside the decide/reveal transaction: a decision that is not durable must not be actioned.
interfaces.notes: `call_rollup_1m` is upserted in the same transaction for tool.call only; approval events are low-volume and are not rolled up.

interfaces.name: guardrails settings (zod fragment)
interfaces.sketch:
// One annotated block in the single settings schema that already generates the
// Settings screen, validates PATCH /api/settings, and feeds search + the cmdk palette.
guardrails: z.object({
  approvalHoldMs: z.int().min(30_000).max(900_000).default(300_000)
    .describe('How long a tools/call waits on the wire for an operator. Most MCP clients '
            + 'give up at 60s regardless; after that the decision still becomes a ticket.'),
  approvalTtlMs:  z.int().min(60_000).max(86_400_000).default(900_000)
    .describe('How long a pending request stays decidable after the caller has gone.'),
  ticketTtlMs:    z.int().min(60_000).max(3_600_000).default(600_000)
    .describe('How long an approval stays redeemable by an identical retry.'),
  denyCooldownMs: z.int().min(0).max(3_600_000).default(600_000)
    .describe('After a deny, identical calls are refused without re-queuing for this long.'),
  maxPendingPerPrincipal: z.int().min(1).max(20).default(3),
  maxPendingGlobal:       z.int().min(1).max(500).default(50),
  requireSecondPerson: z.boolean().default(false)
    .describe('Forbid approving a call made by your own account or key. With a single '
            + 'admin this deadlocks every approval.'),
  webhookUrl: z.url().optional()
    .describe('POSTed once per new request. No arguments are sent. SSRF-validated.'),
  labelling: z.enum(['meta', 'meta+wrap']).default('meta')
    .describe('meta+wrap adds two delimiter text blocks around every upstream result. '
            + 'Only helps clients that honour it; can break clients that expect one block.'),
  secretEgress: z.enum(['block', 'require_approval', 'report']).default('block')
    .describe('What to do when a tool argument literally contains a credential MCPRouter manages.'),
}).strict()
interfaces.notes: No new keep-alive knob: the hold reuses `MCPR_SSE_KEEPALIVE_MS` (15 000) from the existing /api/events stream.

interfaces.name: CLI — mcprouter approvals
interfaces.sketch:
mcprouter approvals list [--pending] [--server <slug>] [--json]
mcprouter approvals show <id>
mcprouter approvals approve <id> [--scope call|tool] [--ttl 15m|60m] [--note "..."]
mcprouter approvals deny <id> [--note "..."]

Session credential only (`mcprouter login`), never a bearer key — it hits the same routes
that reject apiKey principals, so the CLI inherits the property rather than restating it.
Exists so "nobody is watching the console" is an operational choice, not a dead end.
Exit codes follow the existing convention: 1 usage, 2 API error.
interfaces.notes: No `approvals approve --all`. The CLI has the same missing button as the UI, for the same reason.

security: Boundary: downstream caller (the model) -> gateway. Control: the approval queue is capped before anything is written — per-principal 3, global 50, identical `call_hash` deduped into one card by a partial unique index, denied hashes in a 10-minute cooldown. An attacker who can trigger approvals can still create at most 3 cards at a time and each repeat costs them nothing to dismiss.

Boundary: upstream server -> gateway -> model. Control: results are labelled, never judged. The envelope's 110-bit per-result nonce is the only anti-forgery mechanism; without it upstream text closes the envelope itself. Upstream content blocks are never modified, so nothing we do can corrupt a legitimate result.

Boundary: gateway -> upstream (egress). Control: `findManagedSecrets` over arguments, literal + base64 + percent-encoded, blocking by default. The plaintext index lives inside the secret resolver that already holds those values for connect, so the guardrail adds no new reader of `secrets`.

Boundary: operator -> argument material. Control: raw arguments are never persisted; `GET /api/approvals/:id/args` requires operator|admin AND `audit:payload:read`, works only while the call is held, and writes `approval.args.read`. The approval queue cannot become an argument archive even if the database is stolen.

Boundary: API key -> approval authority. Control: all four approval routes reject `principal.kind !== 'user'` before any other check, on top of the settled `disableSessionForAPIKeys: true` and `admin: false` literal type. A stolen mcpr_ key can trigger approvals but can never grant, read or list them.

Bypass — smart routing: `$smart`'s `call_tool` meta-tool dispatches a real tool by name. It must re-enter `guardedCall()` with the RESOLVED inner tool, not call `engine.callTool`. If it does not, every guardrail is one meta-tool away from irrelevant. This is the single most likely implementation mistake in the subsystem and gets its own test.

Bypass — route shape: the guardrail decision is a function of (principal, serverId, bareToolName, args) only. It must not read the route, the group alias, or the exposed name, so `/mcp/s/github` and `/mcp/g/eng` cannot produce different answers for the same call.

Bypass — argument perturbation: a caller can change one byte to get a fresh `call_hash` and dodge the deny cooldown. Accepted: the new call still lands in the capped queue and still needs a human, and the card shows it beside the denied one. A fuzzy fingerprint would trade a real deny for a guessed one.

Bypass — ticket race: two concurrent retries must not both redeem a single-use grant. Enforced in SQL by `UPDATE ... WHERE status='approved' ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED RETURNING`, not in application code, and the resume order is acquire-slot -> re-check-grant -> consume -> dispatch so a 429 never burns a ticket.

Abuse — self-approval: allowed by default, recorded as `self_approved` on the row, the audit event and the card badge. `requireSecondPerson` flips it to a 403. Stated plainly because a two-person team that cannot self-approve cannot use the feature at all.

Abuse — the webhook: `guardrails.webhookUrl` is an outbound fetch driven by settings, so it goes through the same `assertSafeUrl` SSRF guard and per-redirect validation as every upstream URL, and its body carries no arguments. An operator who can set it is already an admin.
Escalation during a hold: a key revoked or a tool disabled while a call waits must not be rescued by the approval. `checkGrant` and `resolveTool` both re-run at resume, before the ticket is consumed.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE POSITIVE — the egress matcher hits a legitimate argument (an operator stored a long file path or a non-secret env value in `secrets`, and a tool legitimately takes it).
failure_modes.behaviour: The call is blocked with a specific message naming the secret label and the JSON pointer, nothing reaches upstream, and a `guardrail.blocked` event records it. The fix is one checkbox: `secrets.scan_egress = false` on that value, surfaced on the server edit screen and named in the error. Install-wide alternative: set `guardrails.secretEgress = 'require_approval'`, which routes hits into the queue instead of refusing them.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE POSITIVE — the policy engine returns require_approval for routine traffic, and the operator is buried.
failure_modes.behaviour: Identical calls collapse into one card (`waiters++`), so a loop produces one row, not a thousand. The per-principal cap of 3 stops varied-argument floods with `approval_queue_full`. The operator's exit is `Approve 15m` on that one (principal, server, tool) triple, which resolves every queued duplicate and is itself an expiring, audited grant. There is no approve-all, so fatigue can never be converted into a blanket permission.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE NEGATIVE — a secret is split across two arguments, double-encoded, or under 16 characters.
failure_modes.behaviour: Not caught, and we say so in the setting's description rather than implying coverage. The audit row still records `inputHash`, `inputBytes` and `inputKeys`, so the call is reconstructible as having happened. Upgrade path is length-windowed hashing per distinct secret length, ~20x slower, deferred until an incident justifies it.

failure_modes.situation: FALSE NEGATIVE — an upstream result carries a genuine prompt injection.
failure_modes.behaviour: We do not detect it and do not claim to. The result is labelled (`_meta` always, envelope on request) and its shape is reported — link count, distinct hosts, odd schemes — so an operator reviewing the audit trail has a signal. If the injected instruction causes the model to make a tool call, that call goes through the full guardrail path, which is where it is actually stoppable.

failure_modes.situation: THE GUARDRAIL ITSELF IS DOWN — the policy engine throws, or the INSERT into `approval_request` fails.
failure_modes.behaviour: FAIL CLOSED. `deny('guardrail_unavailable')`, nothing sent upstream, a `guardrail.blocked` audit event, and an error-level log line. A held call whose DB write fails aborts the hold immediately rather than waiting 300 s for a decision nobody can record.

Nothing rescues the call: it holds for 300 s and then returns `approval_timeout` with the approval id. The row stays `pending` for 15 minutes, so a human arriving later can still approve it, and that approval becomes a 10-minute ticket redeemed by the caller's next identical attempt. Two mitigations exist and neither is a queue: one fire-and-forget webhook, and `mcprouter approvals` in the CLI.

failure_modes.situation: CLIENT DISCONNECTS MID-WAIT (its own 60 s timeout, or the user hit Ctrl-C).
failure_modes.behaviour: `c.req.raw.signal` aborts, the hold stops, the pending budget token is released, and the row is marked `held = false` with no decision recorded. The card shows `caller gone — decision becomes a 10m ticket`. Approving it is still useful and is the normal path for any client with a timeout shorter than ours.

failure_modes.situation: GATEWAY RESTART with calls held, or two operators deciding the same card at the same instant.
failure_modes.behaviour: Restart: in-memory waiters die, every held client sees a dropped stream, which is cancellation by definition in this transport; rows stay `pending` with `held = false` and the 30 s sweep expires them at `expires_at`. Concurrent decide: the `WHERE status = 'pending'` predicate means exactly one UPDATE returns a row; the loser gets 409 with the winning decision in the body and the card re-renders as decided.

deferred.item: MRTR in-band elicitation (SEP-2322): return `InputRequiredResult` with `inputRequests` instead of holding, and let the client retry with `inputResponses`.
deferred.add_when: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ships 2026-07-28. The existing ticket mechanism already backs that retry, so it is a new handler at the HTTP edge and zero schema change.

deferred.item: Per-(server, tool, secret) egress exception rows instead of the single `secrets.scan_egress` boolean.
deferred.add_when: A real install has one secret that is legitimate for one tool and forbidden for another. That is rule-model shape and belongs to the policy-engine agent, not here.

deferred.item: Scanning tool RESULTS for managed secrets.
deferred.add_when: An incident shows an upstream echoing our credentials into model context. Today the next-hop egress scan is the backstop and costs nothing.

deferred.item: First-seen / reputation flagging of domains appearing in results.
deferred.add_when: Operators actually look at the link counts we already report and ask which hosts are new. Needs per-server domain history, which is a table we do not have.

deferred.item: Notification beyond one webhook — Slack app, email, on-call paging, delivery retries.
deferred.add_when: An install reports missed approvals. The webhook plus the CLI covers the on-call case; a retrying delivery queue is a subsystem, not a feature.

deferred.item: Multi-replica approval (pg LISTEN/NOTIFY to wake a hold on another node, advisory-lock pending budgets).
deferred.add_when: We stop being ONE process. Both the semaphore and the pending budget carry the same per-process ceiling today.

risks: The 300 s hold outlives most clients' 60 s request timeout, so in practice the ticket path — not the hold — will be the common route to a successful approved call. If real clients turn out to abandon holds nearly always, the hold is dead weight and (b)+(c) alone would have been the smaller design.
`$smart`'s `call_tool` re-entering `guardedCall()` is a one-line requirement whose omission silently disables every guardrail. It needs a dedicated test, not a code comment.

The redacted `args_preview` may not carry enough for a confident decision on an abandoned card, pushing operators toward approving on thin information; the 256-char verbatim window for scalars is a guess we should measure against real cards.

`secretEgress: 'block'` as the default will fire on some legitimate call in the first month of every install. The one-click `scan_egress` fix has to be genuinely one click or operators will set the whole setting to `report`.
Nothing in v1 stops an operator from approving fast without reading. The bounded window grant reduces clicks but also concentrates trust into a single 15-minute decision.

`labelling: 'meta+wrap'` is opt-in and currently honoured by no client, so the entire labelling half may deliver zero real protection in v1 — it is infrastructure for a host behaviour that does not exist yet.
